    Helping Clients Who Want A Retirement They Can’t Afford (Because Their Prior Advisor Said They Can): Kitces & Carl 203

    November 12, 2026 07:05 am 0 Comments CATEGORY: Kitces & Carl Podcast

    TweetFacebookLinkedInEmail
    LOGIN or CREATE AN ACCOUNT TO SAVE ARTICLE TO YOUR LIST
    • A A A
    LOGIN or CREATE AN ACCOUNT TO SAVE ARTICLE TO YOUR LIST
    TweetFacebookLinkedInEmail
    Table of Contents Navigation
    Executive SummaryVideoShow NotesKitces & Carl TranscriptHow To Deliver Bad News? [01:31]Probability Of Adjustment Scenarios [14:13]How To Adjust Retirement Spending [26:30]

    Executive Summary

    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 33:06
    Instaread

    Retirement signals complex spending, income, and identity shifts, often all at the same time, which is why many clients seek an advisor during this time. Often, as advisors are creating the projections of how a client's retirement may pan out, they have some combination of follow-up questions, good news, and notes of caution. However, sometimes, it becomes evident that a client's lifestyle cannot be maintained with their anticipated retirement timeline… which means it falls to advisors to have this tough conversation.

    In this 203rd episode of Kitces & Carl, Michael Kitces and client communication expert Carl Richards discuss how to help a client who wants a retirement they can't afford – especially if their previous advisor has left them with the impression that they can afford that lifestyle.

    First, advisors may want to minimize 'badmouthing' the previous advisor – even if they are internally exasperated or confounded by the prior analysis.  Advisors may offer to walk the client through what they see instead, essentially "cocreating" or "co-realizing" the possible (negative) outcomes. (And if a client is really stuck on their previous advisor's advice, the current advisor may consider requesting previous meeting notes or other information – just to check what they may have missed!)

    Second, by walking the client through the consequences of their action – and the probability that they'll need to adjust retirement spending – advisors can keep the focus on what, if anything, the client wants to do. Some clients may have enough cushion that they are comfortable with continuing with their current plan, then only adjusting if they need to. For other clients, they may need to consider a broader array of options, from working part-time for several more years to selling assets – and they may need to act with urgency. While these conversations aren't pleasant, it is nonetheless important to remain outcomes-focused and to be clear on how severe the shortfall may be. This helps to avoid both downplaying and catastrophizing the risks and outcomes.

    Even if this conversation is unpleasant, once the potential retirement outcomes are explicit, then the client and advisor can collaboratively brainstorm potential adjustments. Sometimes, the advisor may be surprised by which options the client considers to be "on the table" once it is necessary to make some lifestyle changes. And it can be challenging to anticipate how everyone will genuinely respond in real time when those changes are necessary. A client may anticipate making certain changes, then may opt for different ones when the time comes – for example, they may be more amenable to downsizing their living space than everyone originally anticipated!

    The key point is that adjustments to retirement planning may not be fun, but once the needed adjustments are understood by all parties, then the client and advisor have control again, as they are able to consider their options anew. Advisors will likely need to approach these conversations with a blend of hard analytics and empathy, but when they can "cocreate" a new plan with their client, they can ultimately build something sustainable that leaves everyone happier in the long-term!

    Authors:

    Michael Kitces

    Team Kitces

    Michael Kitces is Head of Planning Strategy at Focus Partners Wealth, which provides an evidence-based approach to private wealth management for near- and current retirees, and Focus Partners Advisor Solutions, a turnkey wealth management services provider supporting thousands of independent financial advisors through the scaling phase of growth.

    In addition, he is a co-founder of the XY Planning Network, AdvicePay, fpPathfinder, and New Planner Recruiting, the former Practitioner Editor of the Journal of Financial Planning, the host of the Financial Advisor Success podcast, and the publisher of the popular financial planning industry blog Nerd’s Eye View through his website Kitces.com, dedicated to advancing knowledge in financial planning. In 2010, Michael was recognized with one of the FPA’s “Heart of Financial Planning” awards for his dedication and work in advancing the profession.

    Read all of Michael’s articles here.

    Carl Richards

    Guest Contributor

    Carl Richards is a Certified Financial Planner™ and creator of the Sketch Guy column, appearing weekly in the New York Times since 2010.

    Carl has also been featured on Marketplace Money, Oprah.com, and Forbes.com. In addition, Carl has become a frequent keynote speaker at financial planning conferences and visual learning events around the world.

    Through his simple sketches, Carl makes complex financial concepts easy to understand. His sketches also serve as the foundation for his two books, The One-Page Financial Plan: A Simple Way to Be Smart About Your Money and The Behavior Gap: Simple Ways to Stop Doing Dumb Things with Money (Portfolio/Penguin).

    Michael: ..."I would say it seems a little bit off." Because he's a protected capital guy. He's like, "This isn't going to blindside us. We're working with you ongoing."     Carl: Yeah. Love that.

    Michael: That's what it was for him. There was a 70% chance that they were on track and a 30% chance that they were going to have to make adjustments, and they were fully prepared to make adjustments.

    Carl: Love that. That's the kind of language we need more of. And by the way, how great is that idea of just being, "If we see this going the wrong way, we're going to have lots of visibility into it." And we've got levers to pull.

    Michael: And so, in that vein, how my approach shifted in handling clients like this, I would then say, "Okay..." Sam didn't say what it is, but just, in general, you get clients like this. So I say, great. So I put that into my planning software, MoneyGuide at the time, RightCapital these days. I put that in my planning software. I pull it up with the client. So the number is whatever. It's 70% probability of success, 30% probability, we're going to have to make an adjustment.

    So then I'll pull out some scenario modeling, right? What-ifs, decision center, or whatever it is, depending on your planning software of choice. So you can see where clients are drifting too far out of whack.

    But to me, the powerful conversation I found was, say, let's put up on the screen, just if the bad stuff's happening, we have to make the adjustments five to 10 years from now. What would it actually take? And sometimes I find it's even surprising from the advisor's end. That's not as bad as I actually thought it was going to be. I remember one of these for a client that at the end of the day, they had a very sizable pension, Social Security, and not a huge portfolio.

    And so what that meant was the incremental spending above their Social Security and pension was pushing their portfolio really hard, but it wasn't a big percentage of their total spending. So they actually didn't need to change their total spending very much to massively change the withdrawals on their portfolio. And we had this scenario where their probability of success was another 75% or 80%. And what it basically came down to is if the bad things are happening, you'll have to sell the lake house.

    And that was enough to completely shore up. And it was not a super big, huge, very expensive lake house, but it was more than enough to sell the whole thing. They're like, "Wait, if the worst-case scenario is when we're 80, we might have to sell the lake house. We're not even sure we're going to be going to the lake house when we're 80. So that's not a concern. We're fine."

    Sometimes it's a modest adjustment. Sometimes it's larger. But I found, A, let's just do some scenario modeling, would do it on the screen with the client in the conference room or screen share, or whatever it is. Let's just see, can you use the what-if scenario tools? How much of an adjustment would it take? Is it 10 grand of spending? Is it 20 grand? Is it 50 grand? Is it sell the vacation home? Is it just a massive change of lifestyle? Is it, we'll have to get a reverse mortgage. But as long as we top the equity in the home, we'll be okay.

    Find out what it is and get to a number. Sometimes that's illuminating unto itself because even from our advisors, I find sometimes the change is not as dramatic as we expected. And then to the extent it is, what I got to that, at least for me, I found was pretty effective with most of the clients in this situation. Once we got some number, all right, the bad things are happening. Looks like we'll have to cut about $32,000 a year spending a decade from now. Just scenario, plan this with me for a moment. If it happens, if we get there, what would you actually cut from your budget?

    What would you do? Hopefully, it'll never come, but you hired me to help you plan. We're planner types. We like to plan. So I just want to have some idea of a plan in place. What would you cut? And what I found through those conversations is some people could answer that with remarkable ease. Oh, that's basically just our fairly vacation budget. We'll just not take as fancy vacations.

    Sometimes they started tapping assets. They didn't say they were going to want to tap, but all of a sudden, if bad things are on the table, they're willing to. It's like, great. Then I know we're going, "We'll sell the lake house. We'll downsize the house. We'll do a reverse mortgage." Suddenly, other things come on the table as possible. It's like, great. If you know what you're going to do, if you know what lever you're going to pull, then I'll find us the planner.

    And then every now and then, we would get someone where they would go through, oh, there's plenty of things you can cut. Cool. Just scenario through this with me for a moment. Let's say some stuff. And they'd say a few things, and we're like, "So that added up to seven. You need to get to 32. What else?" Okay. Now we're at nine. You still need to get to 32. What else?

    And they really couldn't come up with it. And at the point that they said, "We'll just cut our spending later", and then they really could not come up with what they would cut, started change behavior for a bunch of them to say, "I guess maybe we do need to do this later. Now that we're going through the exercise, I'm realizing maybe there's not as much to tap as we thought." But I will say, I guess, owning it from the advisor end, the changes were less severe than I expected, or the client accommodations were actually more manageable than I expected in the overwhelming majority of cases.

    I really adjusted over the years how high of a Monte Carlo projection I anchored to. I liked to see 90% to 95% kinds of things for a long time and came way, way down from that because in going through these exercises, I found the sensitivity to adjustments and the ways that clients can just, if they have to... We're all hoping you won't have to, but if they do have to, are actually more flexible, I think, that we often give them credit for.

    And ironically, although certainly not universally true, many of my bigger-spending clients were also the ones that had the most flexibility to make changes. They didn't want to, but the irony is the high volume of discretionary spending, it's discretionary. They like the lifestyle, but they do have ability to make change in difficult times to tighten their belt if they have to. They're just really hoping they don't have to. And they certainly don't want to give it up out of, "I'm going to give up the things I want to do now because there's a chance I can't afford them later. Why don't I just change them when I can't afford them?"

    Setting An (Articulated) Plan On How To Adjust Retirement Spending If Needed [26:30]

    Carl: Yeah. Look, to kind of put a bow, wrap this up, that's really good. And I think there's two things that are important to me to remember. One is an articulated plan. And I like this in advance. I used to always ask clients, "Hey, if we ever were there, which lever would you want to pull first?" "And remember, you were only talking about spending levers. There's plenty." "Oh, well, the Lake house was not a spending lever. It was an income lever." So...

    Michael: I would start with spending levers. I always started with spending levers. And when they look at what they have to cut, suddenly, sometimes assets come back into play...

    Carl: I remember this crazy cut.

    Michael: ...That weren't in play before. Because, at the end of the day, they really don't want to cut their spending. So, suddenly, they're willing to put certain assets on the table. Great, that worked. You can get the math lots of ways. Just you told me that wasn't on the table, and now it is.

    Carl: Yeah. You could die earlier. There's all sorts of levers that we could... That was a joke.

    Michael: That's a more challenging lever to pull. But, yes.

    Carl: I'm just simply saying an... And the articulated philosophy could be, "I don't want to worry about this right now. Let's talk about this in a couple of years." As long as it's articulated, remember, it's the client's plan.

    Michael: Now you're making it uncomfortable, Carl.

    Carl: I know. You can decide whether you want to be involved in that, but it's the client's plan. The second thing that I think is really important here is that we are notoriously bad as humans at projecting how we're going to handle a scenario. You're terrible at saying, "There's no way I could ever handle a kid." And when you have one, you look at people with two and you're like, "There's no way." And when you get there, you MacGyver-style this stuff together, some bubble gum and duct tape and a paper clip.

    We're actually pretty good at dealing with risky situations when we're in them. We're really, really bad at projecting how we're going to handle them. And I think remembering that, which is what the bond trader guy was essentially saying, "Hey, let's just keep an eye on this." And then one quick last story, because we got to wrap up. I remember having this exact conversation with... This was somebody who made... Their budget was.... I'm embarrassed to even talk about this, but it obviously was not me.

    This is somebody in the movie business, and his budget was seven million dollars a year. That's how much he spent, and he was spending eight. And his team was super nervous about how to break this news to him. And they prepared all these... This is where I heard about it, right? They prepared all these spreads and were asking questions like, how do we break this news? And they went into print, and he's like, "Wait, wait, wait, wait, wait, wait. What did you guys, what? Just get me another movie."

    Michael: You don't cut your spending. You make the income go up.

    Carl: Yeah. "Just give me another movie, and we're set. It's fine." So I think sometimes we got to remember the client might have ideas in their head too. "Sell the lake house, get me another movie, die a little earlier." Who knows what the scenario is, but the client has ideas too.

    Michael: I love it. I love it. Thank you, Carl.

    Carl: Cheers, Michael.
